decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Although the results suggest that spreading of alternatives occurred in all three conditions, the 3 (condition) x 2 (predecision vs. postdecision) x 2 (chosen vs. rejected alternative) failed to show a difference between conditions for the spreading of alternatives. Additionally, self-reported affect was significantly more positive in the action-oriented and positive-nonaction conditions, in comparison to the neutral condition. Using the midfrontal sites reported in the original article, we were able to detect a relationship between condition assignment and greater relative left midfrontal activity. The current study was able to demonstrate greater relative left frontal activity in the action oriented condition as compared to the neutral condition. Correlations between spreading of alternatives and left frontal activation were non-significant. However, the strength and direction of these correlations were consistent with the original study. Commentary Several constraints and differences between the replication and original may have led to the inability to fully replicate the original study.
decisions.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/zpwne/, Harmon-Jones et al. 2008 Study 2 replication), Discussion: Summary of Replication Attempt & Commentary (source_view.json lines 362-363); see also Primary Project Data Study Num 55 (lines 1125-1126)
decisions.reason: While the RPP master spreadsheet records Replicate (R) = 'no' for the single focal 3x2x2 interaction on spreading of alternatives (F(2, 68) = .30, p = .74), the individual primary replication report tests all confirmatory hypotheses of Study 2 and finds mixed results: basic spreading of alternatives occurred in all three conditions, positive affect was significantly higher in the action-oriented and positive-nonaction conditions than in the neutral condition (F(1, 68) = 4.85, p < .05), and greater relative left midfrontal cortical activation was demonstrated in the action-oriented condition compared to the neutral condition (p = .02; planned contrast F(1, 59) = 3.62, p = .06), whereas between-condition differences in spreading of alternatives and within-condition correlations with cortical activation were non-significant, which the authors summarize as an 'inability to fully replicate the original study' (and rate Findings similarity as 'Moderately similar').

decisions.quote: Replication of Poignancy: Mixed Emotional Experience in the Face of Meaningful Endings by Ersner-Hershfield, Mikels, Sullivan, & Carstensen (2008, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology) Thomas Talhelm tat8dc@virginia.edu Minha Lee mhl5b@virginia.edu Casey Eggleston cm5hv@virginia.edu Introduction The authors tested the theory that perceived constraints on future time (feeling like you are near the end of an experience or of life) make people experience more mixed feelings. The theory is that being near the end makes people feel appreciation for the experience, but also sadness that it is coming to an end. We tried to replicate Study 2, in which the authors tested this theory with college seniors on graduation day.
decisions.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/fw6hv/), Title & Introduction (source_view.json line 481); see also References (line 487) and Primary Project Data Study Num 61 (lines 1130-1131)

Addressing the competing_supported_matches pairing flag, the overlap arose only because the same UVA replication team (Talhelm, Lee, & Eggleston) also authored the Rule & Ambady (2008) report (target 51, paired with row 1630) and used the same opening sentence in both Discussion sections; the primary report header, reference entry, and Study Num 61 row unambiguously pair row 1620 with target 39.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Based on the a priori criterion, the replication was not successful. We cannot rule out whether this is because the study was a field study and therefore harder to control. We also cannot rule out whether there is a difference in sample (University of Virginia versus Stanford) that led to the discrepancy. We also cannot rule out whether this replication failed because we surveyed graduates right before the graduation ceremony, as opposed to directly after the graduation ceremony.

(2008) Study 2 (target 39), both the primary project report (t(220) = 0.07, p = .94, d = 0.01; 'the replication was not successful') and the RPP master dataset (Study Num 61, Replicate (R) = 'no') confirm that the replication failed.

decisions.quote: Results Sample characteristics. A total of 222 graduating seniors participated in the study. In order to reach the pre-planned power, we collected data at the graduation ceremony over three years (2012 N = 95; 2013 N = 78; 2014 N = 49). There were 112 participants who received the control questionnaire and 110 who received the “last day” prime.

decisions.reason: With row 1620 resolved to target 39 (Ersner-Hershfield et al., 2008, Study 2), the study collected new survey data from a new sample of 222 University of Virginia graduating seniors to test the original Study 2 hypothesis, which is a direct replication.

decisions.quote: Discussion Summary of Replication Attempt Given the low number of observations, the results of this replication are likely unreliable. Because sufficient power was achieved and the original methodology was followed, however, the results must be reported as part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology. A logistic regression was conducted because the original analysis, a 2x2 between subjects ANOVA, could not accurately analyze data with so few respondents. Confirmatory analysis did not replicate the original finding that participants from the hot list donated more in the to-go condition than in the to-date condition, while participants from the cold list also donated more in the to-go condition than the to-date condition. Although donations from hot list participants did follow the same pattern as in the original study (largely driven by one outlier), the cold list did not, making the interaction non-significant and the results inconclusive. Commentary While this study mirrored the original protocol, it failed to illicit enough responses to draw meaningful conclusions regarding the interaction between commitment and letter focus. Based on the lack of response, further investigation should be conducted with more respondents to test these findings.
decisions.location: Primary Project Report (https://osf.io/download/68m2c/, Koo & Fishbach 2008 Experiment 4 replication), Discussion: Summary of Replication Attempt & Commentary (source_view.json lines 729-730); see also Results (lines 728-729) and Primary Project Data Study Num 77 (lines 1144-1145)
decisions.reason: Although 768,703 solicitation emails were delivered (planned N = 303 donations for 95% power), only 15 recipients donated in total—including just 1 donor in each of the two cold-list conditions—rendering the planned 2x2 ANOVA on donation amount infeasible. The replication authors explicitly state that the ~0% response rate means the results are 'effectively un-interpretable' and 'inconclusive, as an insufficient number of people donated from both variant conditions from the cold list to make any reliable comparisons,' and conclude in Commentary that the study 'failed to illicit enough responses to draw meaningful conclusions regarding the interaction between commitment and letter focus' (and in the RPP master dataset, Study Num 77 is excluded from effect-size and significance-indicator coding 'due to lack of usable data'). Under Rule 1 of the codebook, this is uninformative rather than failed.
